TESTIMONY OF
MAINE ARTS COMMISSION
AMY HAUSMANN, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR
Regarding
LD 109 -- Resolve, Directing the Maine Arts Commission to Study Federal and
National Efforts to Protect Artists from Copyright Infringement by Artificial Intelligence Companies and Users and to Monitor Educational Use
Before the
Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs
February 5, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education
and Cultural Affairs, my name is Amy Hausmann, Executive Director of the Maine Arts Commission.
Maine State government began oflicially supporting the arts in I 933, when the Legislature created the Maine Arts Commission to serve in an advisory capacity to the Governor. In I966, the agency 's scope expanded to support the arts statewide. The Maine Arts Commission fosters and encourages public interest and participation in the cultural heritage and artistic expression of our state. The Commission fulfills the mission through partnerships and collaborations, outreach and initiatives, information sharing, and grants for organizations, artists, and communities throughout Maine.
The Maine Arts Commission, an independent state agency, is governed by a board appointed by the Governor for their interest and experience in the arts and relatedfields. Our new chair, Bob Keyes. was appointed by Governor Mills this summer.
The Maine Arts Commission supports LD 109, presented by Representative Dodge, and we thank her
for introducing it and highlighting the importance of this issue.
As you know, I am new to my role as Executive Director. While traveling around the state meeting
constituents, I heard concerns from illustrators and artists about the threat AI poses to their copyright
protection.

Page 2
The United States is a global leader in AI development, creating new opportunities and economic
growth across industries, including for artists and creators. However, as with any technology, there's a risk of misuse. Research into this issue is critical to address these harms while ensuring innovation is not
stifled.
Reports from the field indicate that tech companies have violated laws by training their AI image tools to mimic the work of illustrators and other artists without consent. These companies encourage users to generate images in specific artists' styles, train AI to write like published authors, or even create music using voices modeled after famous musicians. This misappropriation of style is unlawful and threatens the livelihoods of illustrators, photographers, videographers, filmmakers, musicians, voice actors,
I
writers, poets, animators, cartoonists, songwriters, designers, and actors.
To address this issue in the music industry, in March 2024, the state of Tennessee passed the bipartisan E.L.V.I.S. Act (Ensuring Likeness, Voice, and Image Security Act), an amendment to Tennessee's
Personal Rights Act that sets a precedent for strong protections against unauthorized AI-generated deepfakes and voice clones.
At the time, Dr. Moiya McTier of the Human Artistry Campaign praised the law, saying, "The life's
work and irreplaceable contributions of the creative community to our culture deserve safeguards that
allow AI technology to be used responsibly Without violating anyone's rights or appropriating their art. "
I am no expert on this issue, nor is most anyone in our field, which further underscores the need for
research.
LD 109 presents an opportunity to study this issue and produce a report for the committee by December
2025. This report could help guide legislation to protect the personal rights and copyrights of creative producers in Maine from the unlawful use of their work by generative Al.
The bill directs the Arts Cormnission to conduct a technical and legal study that requires expertise
beyond what is available within the Commission. To accomplish this, we will collaborate with the
Attorney General's Office and hire consultants and advisors. We have provided a fiscal note of $50,000,
which we believe will be sufficient for this purpose.
The arts sector is a $2.2 billion industry in Maine, representing 2.6% of the State's GDP and supporting
18,749 jobs [sources U.S. Bureau ofEconomic Analysis & National Endowmentfor the Arts, 2024]. As
AI continues to transform society, it is essential to establish clear standards that protect the public, ensure transparency, uphold accountability and safeguard the artistic community and creative economy.
A study like this could help us develop and provide information and protection for the creative sector in
our state.
This issue is rapidly growing more complex, and the more information we can gather and share with
Maine's arts community, the better they will be able to protect their copyrights and livelihoods.
Thank you for your consideration of our testimony. I am happy to answer any questions and will be
available for the work session.
